questions.q: In the per-stage latency budget (total 38,361 ms), what percentage of total time is queue wait, and what does that imply about where optimization effort should go?
options: About 99.07% -- effort should go toward reducing queue wait or how often it's paid, not toward the classical prep/post-process stages that together make up a fraction of a percent
About 50%, so effort should be split evenly between queue wait and QPU execution time
About 10%, so classical prep is actually the dominant cost
0%, since queue wait isn't part of the latency budget
questions.explain: Queue wait (38,000ms of 38,361ms total) is about 99.07% of total latency, making it overwhelmingly the dominant variable -- optimizing the 21ms of classical work would have negligible effect on the total.

questions.q: For a 150-iteration run with NO batching, using the 38,361ms per-iteration total, what is the approximate end-to-end deadline?
options: About 95.9 minutes (~1.6 hours), computed as 150 x 38,361 ms
About 40 minutes, based on the QPU execution time scaled up
About 1.6 hours regardless of batching, since batching has no effect on total latency
About 10 minutes, since classical prep dominates
questions.explain: 150 x 38,361 ms = 5,754,150 ms, which is about 95.9 minutes or roughly 1.6 hours -- the honest estimate based on queue-wait-dominated per-iteration timing, not based on the 40ms execution time alone.

questions.q: Why does batching change the 150-iteration latency budget from roughly 29.9 hours (unbatched) to roughly 1.78 hours (batched)?
options: Batching doesn't eliminate queue wait itself, but it eliminates paying that queue wait separately for each of the 17 evaluations per iteration -- all 17 now share one queue wait instead of 17
Batching makes the QPU execute circuits faster
Batching removes the need for any classical pre/post-processing
Batching reduces the number of shots needed per circuit
questions.explain: The underlying per-submission queue wait doesn't change; what changes is how many times it's paid. Batching collapses 17 separate queue waits per iteration into 1, which is why the total drops by roughly the same ~16.8x factor shown in the orchestration lesson.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend when communicating a latency budget to a stakeholder, instead of giving a single confident number?
options: Present a range tied to an explicit assumption (e.g., observed average queue wait), naming the dominant variable so the stakeholder understands why the estimate could change
Always quote the best-case number only, to keep the estimate simple
Refuse to give any estimate at all, since queue wait is unpredictable
Quote only the QPU execution time, since that's the most impressive-sounding number
questions.explain: The lesson recommends naming queue wait as the dominant, variable factor and giving a range tied to that assumption, so a later deviation is understood as a change in device demand rather than evidence the original estimate was simply wrong.

questions.q: If observed average queue wait rises from 38 seconds to 90 seconds, what happens to the batched per-iteration total (originally ~42,750 ms with 38,000ms queue wait)?
options: It rises by roughly 52,000 ms (90,000 - 38,000) to about 94,750 ms per iteration, since queue wait is the dominant term being added once per iteration under batching
It stays exactly the same, since batching makes the system immune to queue wait changes
It decreases, since higher queue wait triggers automatic re-batching
It becomes unbatched automatically, reverting to the ~717,150 ms per-iteration figure
questions.explain: Under batching, queue wait is paid once per iteration. Replacing 38,000ms with 90,000ms in the per-iteration total (150+90,000+680+8 ~= 94,750ms using 40ms x17 execution) shows the new total scales almost directly with the new queue wait value, since it remains the dominant term.
